## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- identify a service boundary from business responsibility and data ownership
- compare a modular monolith with a distributed design
- recognize coupling across APIs, databases, deployment, and teams
- justify when a microservice adds more cost than value

## One business flow, several responsibilities

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Customer[Customer] --> Rental[Rental lifecycle]
    Rental --> Auction[Vehicle auction]
    Rental --> Insurance[Optional insurance]
    Rental --> UI[Rental experience]
```

A useful boundary owns a business decision and the data required to make it.
Technical layers alone do not define services.

## Service boundaries in the repository

| Component | Responsibility | Owned state |
|---|---|---|
| `carRental` | Rental workflow | Rentals and processed events |
| `auctionServiceServer` | Auction execution | Auction runtime state |
| `insuranceService` | Optional insurance offers | Offers and processing history |
| Angular application | User interaction | Transient presentation state |

The boundary remains incomplete if two services must update the same tables.

## Distribution changes the failure model

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    Call[Local method call] --> Same[One process and one failure domain]
    Network[Remote call] --> Delay[Latency and timeout]
    Network --> Partial[Partial failure]
    Network --> Version[Independent versions]
```

Every remote boundary adds operational cost. The business or organizational
benefit must pay for that cost.

## Coupling has several forms

- **Temporal coupling:** both services must run at the same time.
- **Data coupling:** consumers depend on one producer representation.
- **Deployment coupling:** a change requires coordinated releases.
- **Organizational coupling:** several teams must approve one change.

Local code duplication can be cheaper than a shared library that couples every
release.

## Architecture decision

A microservice is a poor default when:

- one team changes the entire feature together
- the domain boundary remains unclear
- independent scaling or release brings no measurable benefit
- operational skills and observability are missing

A modular monolith often provides a safer starting point.

## Module investigation

1. Locate each service entry point in `settings.gradle`.
2. Assign every persisted table to one service.
3. Find one synchronous and one asynchronous boundary.
4. Record one boundary you would merge or split, with evidence.
